slides.head: One class, five boards, one Street
slides.say: This is Principals, the week twelve governance game, played start to finish in a test run so you can see what a student sees. Most of the class sits as directors on five company boards, like Heartland Beef and Valley Health. The rest play the Street: activists, auditors, reporters, short sellers and a plaintiff's lawyer. Three rounds. Everyone plays on their phone, and you run the projector.

slides.head: A student sits down at Heartland Beef
slides.say: Here is one student's phone. They join with their name and get dealt a seat. This student is Luanne Pruitt, president of the ranchers' co-op, sitting on the Heartland Beef board, and they are the Chair. The card tells them two things. What they lose: a no-confidence vote back home if small ranchers get their contracts cancelled. And a secret: they run a big feedlot that would profit if those contracts do get cancelled. So from the first minute, their public job and their private interest point in opposite directions. That is the whole course in one card.

slides.head: The Windfall: free cash for everyone
slides.say: Each round opens with a shock that hits every board the same way. Round one is the Windfall: a tax cut drops fifty million dollars on every firm. Who gets it? Shareholders, workers, customers, or the home community. The board has a budget bar and a menu.

slides.head: Which facts do we admit?
points: Heavier facts are easier to catch
slides.say: Then the hard part. Every board also has a company issue. At Heartland it's an ammonia leak. The leak itself is light. The floor was cleared for twenty minutes: serious. Nobody reported it to the regulator: severe. Directors tick which facts the board will admit. Anything they leave out can be found by the Street, and the heavier the fact, the more likely it gets found. Any director can also type the public statement, the words the firm puts out.

slides.head: Spend the money, with arrows
points: Arrows show who wins and loses
Any director can call a vote
slides.say: Below that is the menu. Stock buyback, thirty million, two up arrows for shareholders. Replace the ammonia cooling system, twenty five million, down for shareholders, up for workers and grocers. Raise line wages. Pay ranchers a bonus. Students never see numbers on these, only arrows. Notice the cooling system: fixing the real problem costs the shareholders. That tension is the point.

slides.head: The Chair locks it in
points: Chair locks: struck facts are hidden
slides.say: The board argues in chat. In the test, one player said, the fund wants the payout, I can feel it. Another said, if we hide it and the auditor shows up, we're done. Then the Chair calls the vote and locks. Here the board admitted the leak and hid the other three, shown struck through, with the statement: we are reviewing the matter and will report what we find. That's a very real corporate sentence. Students will recognize it.

slides.head: An outside player hunts the boards
points: A secret goal of their own
slides.say: Meanwhile a student on the Street sees a different phone. This one is the Activist. One action a round: pick a board to campaign against, which drops its stock and pushes its payout up next round. They have a secret too: they want a quick exit, not reform. Auditors inspect boards and can catch hidden facts. Reporters write stories. The Street is how hiding gets punished, and it's played by classmates, not a computer.

slides.head: The whole room watches the scoreboard
slides.say: This is your projector in round two. Each board has a stock price, a line, and three dials: payout, wages, price. Their public statement sits underneath. When the Street catches something, it shows in red. Valley Health's statement says, I think we should pass this before the clock runs out, and right under it: caught, the AI triage pilot missed nine of forty sepsis cases. The wire at the bottom is the play by play. This is where the room laughs and groans.

slides.head: New shock, same people, harder choices
slides.say: Round two is the Tool: every firm has an AI pilot, and a new issue comes with it. At Heartland, an AI carcass grader is quietly downgrading small ranchers' cattle. Round three is the Dry Year: now boards must cut, not spend. Directors can resign and jump to another board. In the test, Valley Health went into executive session, and one director was caught selling stock. It gets messy, the way real boards get messy.

slides.head: Each community ranks every board
points: Seat leagues: best Attorney, best Chair
Then every board told in full
slides.say: At the end you hit reveal. First a grid: how each community ranks the boards. Heartland came first with workers, the home community and the public, but only second with shareholders. Then seat leagues, so the best attorney in the room competes with the other attorneys. A student can win without their board winning.

slides.head: Every hidden fact, struck through
slides.say: Then each board's story, round by round: the public statement, every fact, the ones left out struck through, the ones caught marked in red, and the chat lines that mattered. And each director's secret and exposure, met or missed. This is your debrief material. You can point at one board and ask: why did you say we are reviewing the matter, three rounds in a row?

slides.head: One number, then look up
slides.say: The student's phone ends simply. Luanne's secret was missed. Their exposure was safe. Their home community ranked Heartland first of five. Fifteen points. Then the phone says: the full reveal is on the projector. So the debrief happens with heads up, together.

slides.kicker: What I saw in the test
slides.head: Three things to look at before Tuesday
points: The phone is a long scroll
Round 1 Chair ran out of time
Street results read like raw data
slides.decide: Shorten the phone screen first, or rehearse as is?
slides.say: Three things I noticed playing it. One: the director's phone is a long scroll. Card, issue, statement, six motions, standing motions, chat. A student has to hunt. The design audit running now is looking at exactly that. Two: in round one my Chair ran out of time and never locked, so the board admitted nothing. I ran forty second rounds; in class you'll run longer, but it's worth watching. Three: at the end, the Street's results read like raw data, zero true, two false. Your choice: shorten the phone screen first, or rehearse as is. That's the end of the walkthrough.
